analysis.one_liner: Bans paying workers less based on sex, race, or national origin for jobs of comparable value.
analysis.headline: The Fair Pay Act of 2013 went nowhere: it never received a hearing or a vote, and in its two years in the House not a single member signed on as a cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended federal wage-discrimination law beyond "equal work" to "equivalent jobs" — work that may look different but requires comparable skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions — and barred paying less for jobs dominated by women or by racial or national-origin minorities. It would have protected workers who discuss wages or file complaints, let them recover compensatory and punitive damages and expert fees, allowed class actions, and required employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more after two years) to report pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. It also applied the same rules to congressional and executive branch employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs disproportionately held by women or people of color — fields like caregiving, clerical work, and food service — whose pay has historically trailed male- or white-dominated jobs of comparable skill and effort. The bill's own findings cite the wage gap (a full-time working woman earned 77 cents per dollar earned by a man in 2009, per the bill text) and note that nearly half the gap cannot be explained by factors other than discrimination. Workers would also gain the right to talk about wages without retaliation, stronger damages, expert-fee coverage, and class-action standing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and minority workers in undervalued jobs

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits paying employees in a job dominated by one sex, race, or national origin less than the rate paid for an 'equivalent job' — work dissimilar in content but comparable in skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions [S3].
Makes it unlawful to fire or punish an employee for opposing wage discrimination, participating in an investigation, or discussing, comparing, or disclosing wages [S3].
Adds compensatory and punitive damages on top of back wages, allows expert fees to prevailing plaintiffs, and permits wage-discrimination suits to proceed as class actions [S3].

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more after two years) to submit pay reports by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, with confidentiality protections, so pay patterns are visible to enforcement and the public [S3].
Directs the EEOC to research, educate, and provide technical assistance to employers and unions on eliminating wage-rate differentials [S2].
Extends the same pay-equity rules to congressional and executive branch employees under the Congressional Accountability Act and the Presidential and Executive Office Accountability Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay different rates for comparable work along sex, race, or national-origin lines: they would face lawsuits with expanded damages, retroactive liability for withheld wages, new pay-data reporting and recordkeeping, and potentially wage adjustments for underpaid job categories. Businesses with modest margins in low-wage, female- or minority-dominated sectors would bear the largest compliance and litigation costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers paying less for comparable work

drawbacks.text: The 'equivalent jobs' standard reaches beyond the existing equal-work rule to dissimilar jobs, which would require employers to run pay-equity analyses across whole establishments and defend any differential under a 'bona fide factor' test that shifts toward the employee if a cheaper alternative practice existed [S3].

Punitive and compensatory damages, expert fees, and class-action treatment would raise the cost and risk of litigation for employers, a cost that could be passed to consumers or absorbed in slower hiring [S3].
The new EEOC pay-reporting requirement, applying to employers with as few as 15 employees after two years, imposes administrative paperwork the smallest covered businesses would feel most [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in underpaid female- and minority-dominated occupations, the bill offered a direct remedy for a pay gap the bill text itself documents, plus practical tools (wage transparency, class actions, fee coverage) that make the remedy usable. The costs fall on employers and are real but standard for civil-rights enforcement: litigation risk, compliance paperwork, and potential wage adjustments. The strongest good-faith objection is the breadth of the 'equivalent jobs' standard, which asks courts and the EEOC to compare dissimilar jobs — a task critics argue is subjective and could produce inconsistent results. Weighing the documented pay gap against those costs, the bill was a substantive pay-equity measure, not a symbolic one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2013 in the House on January 29, 2013 [S1].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 23, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which was the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during the two-year life of the 113th Congress [S4].
No version of the bill was reported out of committee, and the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay lower rates for work done predominantly by women or racial minorities avoided the new pay-equity standard, damages exposure, and pay-data reporting requirements the bill would have imposed. No member other than the sponsor ever had to take a position on it.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2013 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's referral to a subcommittee was its final action

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: House Education and the Workforce subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from April 2013 onward with no recorded action

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition was recorded on the bill itself; the only measurable signal is that the sponsor, a Democratic delegate, drew zero cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-run committee took no action.

industries.industry: Employers generally, especially retail, hospitality, caregiving, and clerical-work sectors
industries.note: The bill would have exposed employers who pay less for equivalent, female- or minority-dominated jobs to back-pay liability, compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and new pay-data reporting. The industries most affected are those with large low-wage workforces segregated by sex and race.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized businesses (15 or more employees after year two)
industries.note: Covered employers would have had to file annual wage reports broken down by sex, race, and national origin and preserve wage-setting records, an administrative burden heaviest for smaller firms.
